evidence_quotes.quote: The basin committees allocate water from the largest and most important reservoirs of the basin

In 1992, state law 11.996 was passed, creating a state system for the management of water resources. The law called for a transformation of the existing system into a more integrated, decentralized, and participatory system
namely, the introduction of water tariffs for water taken directly from rivers or reservoirs.
My research, composed of more than 4 years of ethnographic observation of meetings and more than two hundred interviews with participants and non-participants, reveals high levels of discontent

As an indirect and unexpected result from the introduction of participatory approaches for water management, the state government gained control over the most important water reservoirs of the state, which were previously under the control of municipal politicians.

criterion_notes.c1: No. The study examines river-basin water resource management and bulk reservoir release allocation (competing agricultural irrigation, agribusiness, and inter-basin bulk water uses) in the Jaguaribe Valley, Ceará, rather than household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access (Exclusion Criterion 7).
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording: YES — the paper examines legal, institutional, and governance arrangements in water resources management (Ceará State Law 11.996 of 1992, COGERH, CONERH, participatory river-basin committees, and statutory provisions for licensing and charges on raw water taken directly from rivers or reservoirs). Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: NO — none of the examined mechanisms is a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access; instead, the paper analyzes discursive/semiotic framing in watershed-level bulk reservoir allocation meetings and unimplemented raw-water abstraction charges. Because the paper also fails Criteria 1 and 4 as a bulk water-resources governance study, it is excluded under both the narrow reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Empirical anthropological study based on more than four years of ethnographic observation of basin committee meetings and more than 200 interviews with participants and non-participants in Ceará conducted between 2002 and 2006.
criterion_notes.c4: No. Reported outcomes concern political and symbolic dynamics within river-basin committees—civil society frustration and withdrawal, replacement by municipal technicians, centralization of state control over major reservoirs, and committee vs. rural producer attitudes toward unimplemented raw-water abstraction tariffs—rather than household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or service exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes for the study's own research scope: the population and unit of analysis (river-basin committees and participating/non-participating stakeholders in the Jaguaribe Valley, >200 interviewees), governance exposure (participatory river-basin institutions and modernization discourse), political-participation outcomes, and ethnographic study design are clearly identifiable, though household/community WSS service-access exposure and outcomes are absent.

study_design: Ethnographic qualitative case study (participant observation of river-basin committee meetings and >200 interviews)
population_and_sample: Participants and non-participants in river-basin water committees in the Jaguaribe Valley, Ceará, Brazil (unit of analysis: river-basin committees/meetings and stakeholders; >4 years of ethnographic observation and >200 interviews, 2002–2006)
exposure: Participatory river-basin water resource management institutions (Ceará State Law 11.996/1992, COGERH, basin water allocation committees, and unimplemented raw-water abstraction charges) and state modernization/techno-scientific discourse
outcome: Discontent and withdrawal of civil society participants in basin committees, dominance of municipal water technicians, attitudes toward raw-water abstraction tariffs, and state government control over major hinterland reservoirs (no household or community water/sanitation service access outcomes)
rationale: Excluded as E01 (Wrong topic; see Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). Although empirically rich (ethnographic observation and >200 interviews), the article investigates symbolic modernization discourse and stakeholder participation in river-basin committees allocating bulk reservoir releases (primarily agricultural irrigation vs. agribusiness/bulk transfers) and debating unimplemented raw-water abstraction charges in Ceará, Brazil. It does not examine household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access (c1=no), a rule-type mechanism governing WSS service access (c2 narrow=no; plain=yes for river-basin governance), or any WSS service-access outcome (c4=no).
